utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the registry, the counsel for the Prosecution, the counsel for the Defence. Good morning, General Krstic. We will be resuming our proceedings today. So Mr. Harmon, I see we have a new witness for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my colleagues for the Defence. We have a witness who has appeared previously before this Chamber who provided testimony to the Chamber on the 23rd and the 26th of June using the pseudonym BB. The purpose of him coming back is to examine certain exhibits, specific exhibits. We're not going to repeat his testimony and the procedures and the methodology of intercepting communications that was the subject of his testimony previously. So if I could, Mr. President and Your Honours, if I could have the witness shown Prosecution Exhibit 748 and 788, and I could have copies of those exhibits distributed to Your Honours, then we will proceed with his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to say a few words. Witness BB, you are not going to take the solemn declaration, but I remind you that you are still testifying under oath, and I think you understand what that implies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While I'm waiting for these to be distributed to my colleagues for the Defence, let me just say, Your Honours, that Prosecutor's Exhibit 748 is a copy of a notebook, the original of which I have. I have shown it to the Defence, they have inspected it, and it is available for Your Honours to inspect as well. I could pass this up, if Your Honours please, through the registrar, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness BB, have you had an opportunity to examine first of all Prosecutor's Exhibit 748, which is a copy of a notebook, and have you compared the copy of the notebook to the original notebook? Did you do that in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the Prosecution Exhibit 748 an exact and true copy of the original notebook that you inspected in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, did you examine Prosecution Exhibit 788, which is an extract from the notebook, and did you compare the extract which is found in 788 with an extract contained in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the extract found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 788 an exact copy of what is found in the notebook Prosecutor's Exhibit 748?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, you've had an opportunity to review the notebook, the original and the copy. After having inspected that notebook, can you tell me where that notebook was maintained; at what site? Where was it kept when you wrote your entries into it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the table in the room in which the receivers and recorders were situated, the equipment for monitoring conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to identify that notebook as having come from Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily because I was able to identify my handwriting and I was assigned to Okresanica. Also on the covers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the handwriting of your fellow colleagues who were also assigned to Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to return your attention to a specific conversation, and that conversation in the notebook is found at pages -- it starts at 00804463. So could you turn in the notebook to that particular page, the last two digits of which are 63. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this conversation goes over two pages, ending at page 4465; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm referring specifically to the conversation that starts with a frequency of 255.950, and then the next is, which is the time, 0950. And the correspondents in this conversation are General Krstic, Obrenovic and, in parentheses, Jevdjevic. First of all, could you tell me who recorded that conversation, who captured it on tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recorded this conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the notebook entry about this conversation, is that in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn to page -- turn the page over from the start of the conversation, I'm referring to 00804465. Do you see your name at the end of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read for the record this conversation, and I'm reading from Prosecutor's Exhibit 788. And I'll start at the top: Frequency 255.950, time 9.50, participants General Krstic (barely audible) - Obrenovic - X (Jevdjevic). O: Obrenovic 02 from Palma. X: Go ahead. X: Good. Very good. O: Very good. X: Yes. O: Where is Zepa? X: (Behind us). O: /laughter/ X: It's not yet ours...... (have to) we ... O: What's going on, you gave up Yugoslavia, man. X: Well fuck it, that's the agreement. O: What? Hello? Hey operator, what's happening, did I lose the line? K: Hello? O: Yes. K: This is Krstic. Hello! O: Yes. K: Hey Obrenovic, Krstic here. O: How are you, General, Sir? K: I'm great and you? O: Thanks to you, I am too. K: (You can say that?) And how's your health? O: It's fine thank God, it's fine. K: Are you working down there? O: Of course we are working?! K: Good. O: We've managed to catch a few more. K: Uh-huh. O: Either by gunpoint or on mines. K: Kill them all, God damn it. O: Everything is going according to plan. K: Don't leave a single one alive. O: Yes? K: Not a single one must be left alive. O: Everything is going according to plan. Everything. K: Way to go, chief. The Turks are probably listening. Let them listen, the motherfuckers. O: Yeah, let them, let them. They know what they can listen to. K: Right. Where is your boss? O: He went up towards you. K: When, today? O: Yes. K: This morning? O: Yes. K: OK. OK. Go on. We'll be in touch. O: Can I talk to Jevdjevic for a moment? K: Jevdjevic? O: Yes. K: All right. Since we are ... O: All the best, General. K: I'll put him on. X: Hello. O: (Vitoje?) X: Yes. O: Listen. X: Yes. O: Which road should I use to send a truck in your direction to pick up some cattle? X: And where is that? O: Well, I don't know. My boss told me to give you a call because you know where most of them are. X: Well, the others have already grabbed everything. O: And there's nothing left, huh? X: Not really. O: The motherfuckers are worse than termites. X: Even worse. Now their code-names are Cowboy 1 and Cowboy 2. O: /laughter/ O: Hey, listen ... X: You'll only get some if your guys have caught some and penned them up, no other way. O: OK, then. Where are they? Someone told me somewhere near Milici, right? X: They're in the place where Legenda often carried out searches, and then further up. O: Should I go to Milici? X: (Podravanje and up to Stublic?) O: Uh-huh, to Stublic. X: You'll find them at Stublic. O: OK. X: You know the frequency and there are lots of soldiers and lots of sets, so you can call. O: Good. X: That's it. O: Good. X: And how are you? O: Well, it's OK. X: So long. Let's get together sometime. O: OK. Take care. X: Bye. And that ends the reading of the intercept, the translation of the intercept. That conversation's reflected in your notes in the notebook. Now, in this conversation, Witness, the parties identified themselves, one as Krstic, who's addressed as a General, and the other identifies himself as Obrenovic. Prior to intercepting this communication, were you familiar with the voices of General Krstic and Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the people who were speaking in this conversation, did you recognise those as the voices of General Krstic and as Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the conversation itself there are a number of places, and I'm referring to 788 where there are brackets, for example, at the time, next to the correspondent X, it says, brackets, "Jevdjevic"; and in other locations there also appear to be brackets, for example, on the 8th line down, the words "have to," and further down in brackets, "You can say that?" Do the brackets signify anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: They signify that the intelligibility was low so that I'm not quite certain that what I wrote down is what was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about next to the name Jevdjevic; what do those brackets signify in that particular point in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I intercepted the conversation, the normal procedure was to write down the frequency, the time, and the participants while the conversation is being recorded; and only subsequently, after hearing what was recorded, it is transcribed onto paper. So that during the recording, the participants in most cases were not known from the outset so that in the heading I would mark them as unknown, such as X. And later on, upon listening to the tape, if I established who it was, then I would add the name of that person in brackets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this conversation took place many years ago. Do you have an independent recollection of this conversation or parts of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember parts of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What parts of this conversation do you remember, and could you tell the Judges why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the part when there is reference to the cattle for which they need a truck to load them onto, and then mention is made of cowboy or cow herd 1 and 2 which at the time sounded like a good joke to me, and that is why I remember it. It has stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the course of this interception and the capture of this conversation, you previously described writing, the procedure of writing these conversations down into notebooks. You also described a procedure of sending these by teletype, the content of these conversations, to Superior Command. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 786, distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness BB, do you recognise Prosecutor's Exhibit 786?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is Prosecutor's Exhibit 786?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is in the form in which it was sent from Okresanica to the 2nd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you turn to the conversation we've been discussing, which is on the second page of the B/C/S, and it starts again with the frequency of 255.950 and 0950 hours, and could you then turn -- follow that conversation through to the last page, and you'll see two initials, two sets of initials that appear at the end of that conversation. Is one of the sets of initials your initials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me go to the header on this document, and this document indicates, does it not, the location where this conversation was captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the word "Okresanica"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's a date that appears on there, August the 2nd, 1995. What does that date represent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date represents the day when the conversation was intercepted and recorded and forwarded to the Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn back to the Prosecutor exhibit which is 788 which is the excerpt of the conversation, at the top of the intercept, next to Participants and next to General Krstic's name, there's a bracket that says "barely audible." Can you explain what that notation means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that the participant who was introduced as General Krstic, that he was barely audible. The audibility was far poorer than that of the other participant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges why in radio communications one speaker's voice may appear louder than another's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you need a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can put that on the ELMO, Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to object because, as far as I can see, Mr. Harmon intends to ask the witness about some expert opinion. We have heard an expert opinion on these issues, and if this is going to be an expert opinion that is going to be solicited, then we need to see his report first and then hear him, because this is obviously an expert opinion that Mr. Harmon is going to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree with my colleague that Dr. French did give an explanation as to different frequencies causing different volumes in voices. This witness has worked with radios since he was a ham operator in his youth. He has worked extensively for many years with radios, intercepting communications. I think he is in a position to provide an explanation to the Chamber based on his experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, if the witness speaks only about his own experience, I don't think he can be considered an expert witness. He simply is telling us what his own experience is. We're going to hear the witness, Mr. Petrusic, and after that you will have a chance to cross-examine. Thank you very much. You may continue, Mr. Harmon, but limit it to the actual knowledge and experience of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your experience alone, could you explain to the Trial Chamber why there are speakers with different volumes, one speaker being more audible than another. And if you need to make a diagram on the ELMO, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, we have a participant A and a participant B. The principle of communications was such that participant A is at one location, participant B at another location. Number 1 is the frequency of the signal emitted from position A, and number 2 is the frequency from the location where participant B is situated. I, when monitoring, when I guide my antenna towards participant B, I adjust it to frequency 1, and then I hear -- I can hear quite well participant A. As for participant B, I can hear much less well. Also vice versa; if I were to direct my antenna towards participant B and adjust the receiver to frequency number 2, then the audibility of participant B would be good and that of participant A much poorer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps this could be marked as an exhibit. This could be Prosecutor's Exhibit 858. Thank you for your explanation, Witness BB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, excuse me for interrupting. Witness BB, does that mean that you could choose the participant that you wanted to hear better by adjusting your antenna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you could always only choose one of the two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I had one receiver, only one participant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Harmon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to play two tape recordings for you. You had an opportunity to listen to these in my office, but I'd like you to listen to them again in Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could have -- these are two tape recordings of the same conversation, and if we could start, and we'll play these successively. We'll play the first conversation, which is already an exhibit. It has already been played in this Chamber. It is Exhibit 789. And for reference, this is tape 48 that was referred to in Dr. French's report on page 5. So if we could play Prosecutor's Exhibit 789. There should be a transcript of that already available. It is 789/A and B. But the purpose of this exercise is just to listen to the volume. So if we could play, please, 789.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do the interpreters interpret? Because we don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary to interpret. This is only to listen to the volume of the speakers. So it's just to listen to the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's very soft. I'm not hearing it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm not hearing it at all either.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. The director just informed me that he can hear it, but obviously we can't, and he's adjusting that immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The director just informed me that the engineer is on his way and it will be less than one minute before it begins to play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, can you leave that part of the testimony for the time being and we can come back to it later?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, at the conclusion of this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the conclusion of this exercise, Mr. President, I was going to move to an entirely different conversation which will take me out of the area of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can act differently. We have been working for almost 45 minutes, so perhaps we can have a 15-minute break now and come back. I see positive signs from the technical booth, so let's have a 15-minute break and then we'll come back. --- Break taken at 10.01 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, I think that we are now able to hear the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll play two recordings back to back. The first one will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 789, and if we could play that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness BB, whose voice was louder in that tape, Obrenovic's or Krstic's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this tape, the voice of Obrenovic was louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if we could play the next exhibit, a new exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 835.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we ought to interrupt at this point because the question that is being asked here is -- let me say that the Judges aren't able to know whether the -- it is distortion from the technical booth or whether the distortion is on the original, so we're hearing this badly. And it's up to Mr. Harmon to tell us, was the distortion due to the technical facilities here or on the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Quality, we have the original. We'll bring the quality -- the original down here, and we'll put it on the machine and we'll play the original, but that will take just a few minutes. I could continue with my examination, but in the meantime if I can get a message upstairs, we will get the original down here. I apologise, Mr. President. This was supposed to be a fairly short exercise. It looks like it's going to be a longer exercise, but we will bring the original down; we'll put it on. The witness -- let me ask the witness this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness BB, have you heard the tape recordings, the two tape recordings in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you heard the originals as well as the copies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of the tapes that you heard of a different -- I'm sorry. Were there differences between the two tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there differences in the volume of the voice of General Krstic in those two tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the tape where General Krstic had -- I'm sorry, let me rephrase that question. Could you identify which of the two tapes was more likely to have come from Okresanica, after having listened to both the original version and the copy of the same conversation from two locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of the tapes were you able to identify as likely having come from Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tape on which General Krstic's voice is less audible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That would be, Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit 789, which is again referred to in Dr. French's report at page 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did anybody else at Okresanica copy -- record this particular conversation, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me put to you a question. General Krstic has heard this tape. He has asserted that this tape is 100 per cent montage. I'd like your comments on that proposition.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, in 1995, I heard that conversation and recorded it. Now, whether this concrete tape here is the tape that I actually recorded on, I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are there factors that led you to conclude that it may be the tape that you actually heard and recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the recording on this tape completely corresponds to my notes in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, then, I will await the arrival of the tape, we'll put the original on, Mr. President. Again, I apologise for the delay. We'll now turn to a different subject, and if I could have -- if the witness could be given, please, a copy of Prosecution Exhibit 843 and 842/A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President and Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit 843, as you will see, is a copy of a notebook, and 842 is a copy of an excerpt from the notebook. The original notebook I have. I will ask the registrar also to distribute that to Your Honours for inspection. And in the notebook, the original notebook, you will see, Your Honour, a blue tab, and the blue tab is only to mark the location of the excerpt that is Prosecutor's Exhibit 842. This original notebook also has been given to the Defence for their inspection. Now, there is one other piece of information that Your Honours need to know about this particular exhibit, and this notebook confirms a printout of the same conversation which is found in three separate Prosecution exhibits. The printout of this conversation is found in OTP Exhibit 364/1/13 July/tab 16. The printout is also found at OTP Exhibit 529 and at OTP Exhibit 404, tab 341. With that background, then, Your Honours, I'll proceed with my examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness BB, have you had an opportunity to examine the original notebook in my office and compare it to the copy, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 843, and can you tell the Judges if the Exhibit 843 is a true copy of the original?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is to say, I had occasion to look through it, and I agree that this copy is a true copy. It corresponds to the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does Prosecutor's Exhibit 842, which is an excerpt of a conversation, correspond to, exactly to the entry that is in the notebook that is found at page 01077793 and -94?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after having inspected Prosecutor's Exhibit 843, can you tell me, is this a notebook from Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on what basis do you make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the fact that I recognise the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise my own handwriting and some other handwritings of my colleagues who were with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to Prosecutor's Exhibit 842 and ask you about this specific conversation which is found in the notebook at 01077793 and -94. Did you capture that conversation on tape? Did you actually record that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make the entry in the notebook relating to that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you date this conversation? Did we go through that exercise of attempting to date this conversation in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take a look at the notebook. If you need the original, we can pass the original to you. I think you may need the original, actually, to make the dating because there's ... If you refer to page 7770. I could assist you if -- if you turn to page 7770, which is the cover, and you turn to page 7798. Do you see dates on those respective pages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date on 7770?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th of July, 1995. And on page 0017798 it is the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based on those two dates which bracket the conversation, can you tell the Trial Chamber when you believe that conversation occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the conversation occurred between the 12th, therefore, and the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me briefly read this conversation into the record. I'll start reading: 785.000, Channel 5, at 2040 hours. (General Krstic X - Y (Borovcanin from the specials) X: Hello, Krstic/here/. Y: Hello, Borovcanin/here/, General, how are you? X: Well, where the fuck are you? Y: I'm here at the command post. X: How's it going? Y: It's going well. X: Don't tell me you have problems. Y: I don't, I don't. X: And Krstic also ....., went somewhere towards you. Y: That's exactly what I want to know. X: ...... Y: Is there anything for us from you? X: Work on this part -- and then "which" has a line through it -- ... Y: Yes. X: ... Y: At the moment. X: ... Y: We'll continue that tomorrow. X: ... Y: All right, bud. X: OK, we'll be in touch. And that concludes the reading from Prosecutor Exhibit 842.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this conversation, General Krstic is identified as "General" and Borovcanin is identified by name. Let me ask you this question: In this conversation General Krstic's name appears in brackets, as does Borovcanin. Can you explain those brackets, what they mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, when the conversation started, when I came, at the beginning of this conversation, the device for recording is switched on and we write in the participants, the particulars in the heading. So at that point I was not sure who the participants in the conversation were, so I wrote in "X" and "Y." And later on, when I listened to the tape again, and when I recorded it in my notebook, I realised who the participants were and therefore put them in in brackets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you: In respect of the words "from the specials," what does that mean? What does that signify, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means -- that refers to the special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. I have received a note about this tape, but I would like if I could have a break for a few minutes, or I could play it later or after the cross-examination. I just needed to make sure that the correct sequence is found and played.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed it is ready, so this is the recording of Prosecutor's Exhibit 835 from the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This apparently is not the conversation -- if we could have a few minutes, I'll make sure the correct selection on the master tape is found. I've concluded my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Harmon, what you have just suggested was that we do the cross-examination now and then afterwards you will play us this part of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. What I would suggest is since the purpose of playing the tape is for Your Honours to listen to the different qualities and the different volumes of the various speakers - in one case General Krstic is softer and in another case he's louder - it's only for purposes of Your Honours' listening to the two tapes. We can do that with or without the witness present. At this point I've examined him about his having listened to both of these and his having made a selection as to which one was more likely to have been intercepted at Okresanica. He doesn't have to listen to the tapes themselves. But I'm at the Trial Chamber's disposal as to how it wants to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic -- Mr. Visnjic, have you any remarks to make regarding the suggestion that we have just heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, no comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Madam Registrar, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. I just received a call from the booth, and both case managers apparently are in the booth and they've identified the correct portion, so we can begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. Then let's begin and finish this part of the exercise. I'm happy to have it played now if it's ready and they have selected the proper selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I be permitted to ask the witness a question about this, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've heard this tape now which is Prosecutor's 835. Can you tell me which voice is louder and which voice is softer; General Krstic's or Obrenovic's? I'm sorry, which voice is louder; General Krstic's or General Obrenovic's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic's voice is louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I meant to say Obrenovic. I think I promoted Mr. Obrenovic to the rank of General, so it should be "Obrenovic" and not "General Obrenovic." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Visnjic, your witness for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness BB, could you please take Prosecution Exhibit 748 and turn to page ending 00804463. In response to Mr. Harmon's question, you explained that the conversation beginning on that page was recorded on the 2nd of August, 1995. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 00804465.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next conversation that follows this one, was it recorded on the 7th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that between the 2nd of August and the 7th of August, 1995, no entries were made of intercepted conversations in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that also mean that there were no additional conversations taped on this tape between the 2nd and the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several notebooks being used simultaneously so that when the operator who was transcribing from the tape, he would take the first notebook at hand and transcribe a conversation in it, so that it was quite possible for nothing to be taken down in a particular notebook for a day or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this happen often or rarely? How many notebooks did you have in front of you when you were working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several, let me say five at least, so that this happened quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question by my learned friend Mr. Harmon, you said that you were able to identify the conversation recorded at Okresanica when you received both tapes. Did you remember whose voice was louder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I took note of in addition to the actual facts, the information, what I heard, the brackets, question marks, full stops and commas, with regard to the parts of the conversation that were less intelligible and comparing the recording with the transcript from those days, I established that the recording fully corresponds to the transcript in the notebook in terms of audibility and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified in this courtroom on the 23rd and 26th of June. Do you know why you were not questioned about this particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at Exhibit 843, please. This is the second notebook, and will you look at the page beginning with 01077815.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a conversation which is said to have started at 10.51. Are we looking at the same page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the Prosecution, you said that you recognised the handwriting of your colleagues. Do you recognise the handwriting of this person who took down this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say with certainty regarding the handwriting. I think I know the initials of the person who took it down and the initials of the signalsman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to give us their names because of protective measures. This answer will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I should like to read out this conversation because I have several questions for the witness afterwards. And this conversation is in Serbo-Croatian, so for the transcript I should like to read it. 10 hours 51, X, Y, Bogicevic - General Zivanovic. X: Hello. Y: Hello. X: Is Zivanovic there? Y: Yes, and who needs him? X: Bogicevic from Belgrade. Y: Just a moment, please. X: Hello. Just a moment, General, you're wanted. B: Hello. Z: Hello. B: Zile, hi. Z: Hi, Bogi. B: Good luck. Z: Thank you. B: Here I have the truck. Five tonnes of goods are here for you in Ljubovija. Z: Yes. It's the same as if you were in Belgrade. B: What should we do now? That is what Triso told me. Z: I beg your pardon? B: Triso told me to do that. Z: Triso doesn't know anything about borders. B: Yes. Z: If that is what he told you to do, report to him and then pass it on to me. B: We want to drive some stuff over there to you, but ... Z: Where? B: Over there where you are, up there. Z: I am now in Belgrade. B: Oh, I see. Z: I have liberated Srebrenica and now I have been given a new assignment. B: Yes, yes, fine. Z: How are you? B: Very well. I am coming up there. Z: I have no home. B: I'll come up there now to bring you some watermelon to cool off with. Z: Do that. B: Fine. Z: And how are my people, my Serbs? B: Fine (Krile?) mine. Z: Everything is fine. Say hello to the Serbs. B: I will. Be well. We'll be in touch. Z: Fine. B: Bye-bye. Witness BB, according to your theory for the determination of dates, could you determine when this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: By looking at the dates in this notebook, I can say that the conversation took place between the 15th of July and the 18th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness BB. Mr. President, the Defence has no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I have just a minute to look at this document? Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness BB, would you take the document that you've just been examined on, and I'd like to refer you to page 01077811. And on that particular page there is a date of July 15th, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say the conversation took place between the 15th of July and the 18th of July, would you turn to page 01077846. Do you see a date of July the 18th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from July -- that date, at that entry point where that date is, the conversations that follow are the conversations that were intercepted on the 18th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, and the conversations, turning back to page 01077811, are the conversations that were intercepted after the 15th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the first conversation that was taken down into this notebook, and it occurred on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I've had an opportunity to look at many of these notebooks, and let me ask you this: Are the conversations that are intercepted, is there a time referenced in respect of each of the conversations that is intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we turn to page 01077811, the first conversation that was noted in this notebook on the 15th of July occurred at 055 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 5.54 hours. I'm sorry. Okay. So that's early in the morning. And the subsequent conversations -- can you go through this notebook, starting at this page where the first conversation is, and tell me when you believe the 16th of July is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of July could roughly have begun on page 01077819.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges why you believe the 16th of July could start at that particular page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the conversation prior to that that was intercepted has a time indication of 11.02 a.m., and this conversation on page 01077819 has the time 6.19 in the morning. So most probably the next day in the morning. It could have been one of the first conversations, because the date is indicated. Probably the first conversation that day is contained in one of the other notebooks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you believe to be the 17th of July, where that starts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th of July I think begins on page 01077833.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that? And why is that that you believe it occurs on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation on the previous page has a time indicated, 2203 hours, so that means in the evening. And then this conversation has a time noted as 7.57 in the morning, so that means the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you just look from that particular page which ends in 833, over to page 846, to see if the times that are noted in respect of each of the conversations continues to get later and later and later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Until the page 01077846, on which the date is indicated of the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turning to the conversation about which you were examined, which is found at page 815 and 816 - I'm sorry - 815, yes, and 816, and having noted that before that is the date of the 15th of July, 1995, and after that, on page 01077819, you believe to be the date of the 16th, are you able now to more precisely give the Trial Chamber a view as to when the conversation about which you were examined occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation certainly occurred between the 15th and the 18th, of course, including the 15th, but it is my opinion that it could have occurred on the 15th. So it is my opinion that this particular conversation occurred on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Judge Fouad Riad, you have questions? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness BB. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to understand a few things from you. You mentioned in an answer to the Prosecutor that you were familiar with the voice of General Krstic and Obrenovic, and you said, "I was familiar with their voices at the time." What made you familiar with the voices? Did you listen to them in tapes or on the radio, or meet them? What made you familiar with their voices?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Judge Riad, for interrupting, but General Krstic needs to take a break, so with your permission, can we take a 20-minute break and we'll reconvene for the Judges' questions. I apologise for interrupting you, Judge Riad. Let us take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we proceed? Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness BB, I'll repeat my question. You mentioned that you were familiar with the voices of General Krstic and Obrenovic. How did you become familiar with their voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995 I worked as an operator on the monitoring of those conversations and their recording and so, doing those jobs, I was frequently in a position to hear those voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just, can I just know the monitoring office where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you always heard their voices through your interceptions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And was it always the same voice whenever you heard it? It was always the same voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was never different? One day you would say, "Is it, is it General Krstic or not," because there was never a face-to-face or direct contact, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case of doubt, I would usually make a note of that in my notebook, and then I would consult my other colleagues if I wasn't quite sure myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So there was a very important, very important means of verification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was essential to verify the participants in a conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And sometimes you mentioned that you would put the names between brackets. That would be in case of doubt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case of doubt, I would place a question mark beside the name which was in brackets. And names in brackets alone meant that when I listened to the tape again, they were written in, entered into the notebook afterwards, after I had listened to the tape again and not when I listened in to the conversation the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in one of your answers you mentioned that if you have one receiver you can hear only one person better, better than the other. Now, what happens if you doubt the other; what do you do in that case? Do you adjust the receiver, or you can only be sure of one person, not the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only be certain of one speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in a case like, for instance, an interception where one voice was clear, which we happened to have heard, and the other was not clear, what do you do in such cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases of that kind, in my notes, in my notebook, I would denote that the other participant was not clear, not audible, and that is what I would do. I would make a note of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then what is the follow-up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, it was noted that some of the participants were heard less well or not at all. And if you cannot identify the speakers, then you say that you were not able to perform identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, would there be a chance of comparing it with other interceptions? Would other interceptions be made at the same time and you try to find out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to do that. I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there somebody who does it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know. Maybe, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness, at the time that you heard the intercept 788/A on August 2nd between General Krstic and Obrenovic and Jevdjevic, can you estimate how many times you had previously intercepted conversations in which General Krstic was a participant? Just a rough -- I mean, say, one, a dozen, a hundred; just how many conversations you had intercepted in which he had participated, you had heard his voice before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but a number of times, perhaps several tens of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That's good enough. Thank you. Now, in both of the conversations that you have been examined about in which General Krstic is alleged to have been one of the participants, in both of the conversations somebody identifies themselves as General Krstic. They say, "Hello, I'm Krstic," or, "Krstic here." When you were intercepting the conversations and later writing down your versions of them, did you rely more on the self-identification by the person who said they were General Krstic or on your voice recognition, or was it a combination of the two? Which would you say you relied on more heavily; the fact that they identified themselves as a particular person or your independent recognition of their voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rely more on their own self-introduction, although I used both for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the August 2nd conversation with Obrenovic and Jevdjevic, did you, even though at least one of the versions was barely audible, General Krstic's voice was very audible [sic], did you perceive anything different about the manner in which he spoke based upon your having heard him before? Did anything remain in your mind that he sounded any different, since you said you had heard him tens of times before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: This second conversation, that is, the one that I did not record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was only a few days ago that I heard it. After so many years, it would be difficult for me to recognise the voices exactly, but at the time when I listened to those voices frequently, I was able to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was whether, even recognising the voices at the time, you felt or heard anything different about the way in which the General spoke in that one intercept. Did he sound any different than he had sounded in other intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked what parts of that August 2nd conversation, or why you remembered it, and you told Mr. Harmon you remembered the talk about the cattle and the cowboys. My question is: The rest of the conversation, or another part of the conversation had these phrases like, "Kill all the Turks," or whatever the phrase was, "Don't let a single one of them stay alive." Did that not remain in your mind? Did there not seem anything unusual about that, that you would remember that as opposed to the bit about the cattle and the cowboys? Was that the sort of thing you didn't pay much attention to because you heard it from a lot of different sources?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts like that, conversations where killings were mentioned, I had heard hundreds of times before that, and that was usual for me to hear that kind of thing, whereas the thing about the cattle and the cowboys seemed to me to be a good joke at the time and I remembered that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. And my last question is in regard to the second conversation that you were questioned about between General Krstic and Borovcanin. One thing -- I just want your comment on this. Again, the transcript says that General Krstic identified himself in the beginning, "Hello, Krstic here," and the conversation is very fragmented, with many dots. I mean, it's very hard to get much sense of what it's about. But were you not surprised, or what was your reaction to the fact that in the middle of the conversation the person who is alleged to be General Krstic refers to Krstic; in other words, he refers to, if it is himself, in the third person. Would you not have expected him to have said "I" or "me" or "myself" rather than using the third person, and did that not raise any doubt in your mind in a conversation which is so full of dots and so -- all the rest of it is -- for the rest of the page it's all dots; there's nothing else that's intelligible that's attributed to him? Did you think about that? Did it give you any concern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was doubt, yes. And everything that I doubted, that I was not sure of, I either jotted it down or, most frequently, I would consult my other colleagues, who at that point had a little more experience on the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So if that figured among your doubts, you would have gone and consulted with your colleagues and resolved the doubts in favour of attributing the conversation to him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if my doubts were cleared up. But if the doubt remained, if I was still unsure, then I would denote that too. I would say that those facts had not been cleared up, and that is how it would go on to the Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But we are then to infer from the fact that you didn't record those doubts that your own doubts were resolved as far as this second conversation between Krstic and Borovcanin? You didn't send on anything to the Superior Command saying, "I've still got doubts, unresolved doubts, about this," did you? You didn't? You didn't send anything on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Witness BB, I too have a few questions for you. The first question is the following: How long, how much time, had you been working up until the time you listened in to this communication between supposedly General Krstic, Obrenovic, and Jevdjevic? How many times before that -- how long had you been working before that? How long were you working on intercepts before you intercepted that particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Okresanica from about the beginning of May 1995, in that location, although I had been doing the same sort of work at another location, that of Konjuh. I had been there one year before that, one year previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in total, how much experience had you had on these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally had been working for a little more than a year in work of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. So if I understand correctly, you were able to identify the voices because the interlocutors either said the names, gave their names; but were there any other characteristic features which would lead you to identify a particular voice, and in particular, that of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time each of the operators was able, to a fair degree of certainty, to recognise the voices of the participants, the ones we focused on in the conversations, which means that all the higher officers of the army of Republika Srpska. And all the conversations that were recorded were listened to several times, a number of times, by the operator, and several times during the day. So these conversations were recorded and they were heard and played over again and again so that they were the voices that the operators had been accustomed to, and then after several months of working in this way, you would be able to recognise the voices very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. And now another question. We have seen the notebook. Let me just find it. I think it was the Defence counsel that asked you a question with respect to the intercepts and intercepts of conversations which did not -- between the 2nd and 7th of August, and you said that in that notebook the intercepts had not been recorded; they did not exist between that period. Now, my question is, if we take a look at the entirety, at all the notebooks in this time frame, would it be possible to find other notebooks with intercepted messages between the 2nd and 7th of August? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have all the notebooks that existed at that time in that locality in the field, I could with certainty ascertain the date of each conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, very well. Another question for you, Witness BB. You said that you knew the handwritings of your colleagues. Did you know them in 1995, or do you recognise them now, today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the handwritings I can partially recognise today as well, but the initials, the signatures and that kind of thing, I can certainly recognise today too because I had a lot of occasion to see them, and they have lodged in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now another point, another question. In some of the intercepts we see -- for example, if we look at Exhibit 788, it is the intercept supposedly between General Krstic, Obrenovic, and Jevdjevic, the text says, for example - and it says in English, I'm looking at the English version - "The Turks are probably listening. Let them listen." Did you hear that expression or that idea several times, or was it very rare, if I can put it that way, to hear an expression like this used, indicating that other people were listening in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have occasion many times to hear that, especially from the operators and their signalsmen, and they would caution and warn that there was the possibility of tapping in, people tapping in to the conversation, tapping in to the participants in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another question, to wind up with, Witness. You gave an answer to Judge Wald a moment ago and said that the expression "kill them all" did not particularly grab your attention because you had heard that frequently. My question now is the following: Did you hear that expression frequently - and you'll explain afterwards what you mean by frequently - coming out of the mouth and with the voice of General Krstic? Did you hear that expression from his mouth and in his voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: From General Krstic I did not hear that often, but I did have occasion to hear on a fair number of occasions, and even when I worked as a signalsman, I would receive written documents where that was written. It would be written fairly frequently. And that is why, as I said, it had become -- I had become accustomed to it, to that type of information. But in concrete terms for General Krstic especially, no. As far as I can remember, I could not hear that often, and perhaps that was the only time that I had heard him say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, very well, Witness BB. We thank you very much for coming back to the Tribunal, and we wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence and to your work. I see Mr. Harmon on his feet. I suppose you're going to tender documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, we would like to tender the following exhibits: Prosecutor's Exhibit 748, which is a notebook, we would ask that that be tendered under seal because of the name of the witness that is included in it; 788 is an excerpt; we would submit 786 which is a printout, we would ask that that be admitted under seal because of the initials of the witness that are on that; 789, which is a transcript of tape 48 -- I'm sorry, which is tape 48 and the transcripts; Prosecutor's Exhibit 835, which is tape 32 and the transcripts; Prosecutor's Exhibit 843, which is a notebook, we would ask that that be admitted under seal because of the names of people in it; 842, which is an excerpt from that notebook; and lastly, Prosecutor's Exhibit 858, which is the diagram drawn by Witness BB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, any objections or comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence opposes the admission of these exhibits regarding the notebooks on the grounds given by Mr. Petrusic in his previous statement and which are to be found on pages 4718 to 4723 -- 4711 to 4723, so as to avoid repetition. These are reasons that this Trial Chamber has been informed of by Mr. Petrusic. Also regarding tapes and excerpts of conversations from those tapes, the Defence particularly objects to those exhibits, the reasons having been given in our motion for the exemption of these exhibits from the rebuttal case as we feel that they are not appropriate for rebuttal. Those would be, in brief, our objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If I could just clarify, you -- I have read all your papers, but they have been over a long period of time, and I just want to clarify the grounds of your objections. Your grounds are still -- we have ruled on the statement portion, but your grounds are still authentication, are they? You raised that initially, and you raised the appropriateness of bringing them up in a rebuttal rather than a case in-chief. Are those the two main grounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our objections regarding authenticity of these exhibits are based on the grounds given by Mr. Petrusic on pages 4718 to 4723. These relate to the written documents. As for the tapes, themselves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- our objection is again based on lack of authenticity, or rather, inadequate evidence to prove authenticity, and also that that type of evidence, and bearing in mind the criterion of authenticity which would be adequate for the Court, we feel that they should not be admitted. So our objection regarding authenticity applies to all these exhibits, both tapes and written documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But just to make sure I understand: Putting authenticity aside, you are still objecting that they shouldn't have come in on rebuttal or you're not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon, anything new to add, having heard what Mr. Visnjic has just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. I understand the objections. Those objections do not apply to, I assume, Prosecutor's Exhibit 858, which is a hand-drawn diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my mistake, Your Honour. The objection does not apply to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Now let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is no doubt regarding Exhibit 858, so that exhibit is admitted into evidence. With respect to the other exhibits, they are linked to the decision that the Chamber took yesterday. In other words, when the Chamber decides on the Defence motion, then these decisions will be considered in the same context, and I take advantage of this opportunity to inform the parties that we have felt some doubts regarding our decision yesterday - rather, that certain clarifications are necessary - and that is why we're going to review that decision and perhaps tomorrow give you explanations and possibly also to give you a decision in writing. So in any event, we will communicate to you tomorrow. There are some things that are already clear in yesterday's decision, but there are others that may be under doubt, and we felt that the parties needed some clarification, and we are going to clarify that decision tomorrow and possibly, as I have already told you, give it to you in writing so that the time for the appeal will be counted as of the time the written ruling is issued, if there is one. So for the moment that is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the decision of the Chamber, in other words, that these exhibits will be considered in a package with all the others. Witness BB, thank you very much, once again. Please don't move so that the usher can pull down the blinds for you to be able to exit safely. So Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, I think there are some exhibits from yesterday. Perhaps we could take advantage of the time to clear up certain things, to clean up any outstanding issues. So could you tell us what they are, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have my colleague, Mr. McCloskey, address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. We do have some exhibits. One would be Dr. French's C.V., which is 840; Dr. French's speech report, 839; and his audio report, 838. We would ask that 839 and 838 be entered under seal because of some of the information and people it contains. And then Exhibit 841, which was the C.V. of Witness EE, we would ask for under seal, and as well as the diagram of Witness EE, which I would also ask be entered in under seal. And as far as I see, that is all the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, and the diagram of Witness EE, it is Exhibit -- what is the exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. So Exhibits 838, 839, and 841 will be admitted into evidence under seal. The other exhibits, 840, 841 - no, sorry - 840 and 847, those two will be admitted also into evidence. Have I forgotten anything? Have I left anything out, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon, I don't know whether you would prefer to have a lunch break now or should we begin? Perhaps let's begin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, we can begin. We have another witness, protected witness, so we will have to lower the blinds while he comes in. I can tell Your Honours this will be Witness Z, and Witness Z testified before the Trial Chamber with protective measures on the 22nd of June, 2000. Again, he will be a protected witness. In his testimony today he will have face distortion and he will continue to use the pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, you're telling us that those will be the same protective measures that the witness had in June. Is there any objection by the Defence? Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the Chamber grants and maintains the same protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness Z. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good afternoon. I hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You remember being here on the 22nd of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you also remember taking the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I wish to remind you that you're continuing to testify under oath. You know what that means. So you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now be answering questions by Mr. Harmon, whom you know very well, and he is standing to your right. Mr. Harmon, your witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness Z. I'm going to be referring to you by your pseudonym that you used previously in your testimony in June. We're not going to go over all of your testimony. We're going to be focusing today on certain exhibits. Before we focus on those exhibits, let me ask you, just to refresh the Judges' recollection: You were an intercept operator at which location in June, July, and August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a location near Banovici called Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 747 and 787 shown to the witness, please, and distributed to the Trial Chamber. For the record, Your Honours, Exhibit 747 is a copy of an original notebook which has been shown to the Defence, which has been shown to the witness, and which I have here in my possession. I'd like to pass it up to the Chamber for their inspection as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Z, did you have an opportunity in my office to examine the original notebook and the copy of that notebook which is marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 747?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on those comparisons, can you tell the Judges whether the Prosecutor's Exhibit 747 is an exact and true copy of the original notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also examine Prosecutor's Exhibit 74 -- I'm sorry, 787, which is an extract of a conversation from the notebook 747?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the conversation and the pages that are found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 787 exact copies of what are found in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having identified and having examined the notebook, both the original and the copy, can you tell me at what intercept site that notebook was filled in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the location of Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on what do you base that opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base it on the fact that this is certainly my handwriting, I recognise it, and I know that in that period I was at that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could turn your attention, please, to the notebook pages 00804430 and -431.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see a conversation in the notebook that starts out with --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- frequency 245.950, taken at 9.50 hours, with participants General Krstic and Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you record the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then make a notebook entry relating to that conversation in this notebook 747?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read for the record the translation of the notebook entry. I'll start now: Frequency: 245.950. Time: 9.50. Participants: General Krstic - Obrenovic. K: Hello Obrenovic, Krstic here. O: How are you, General, sir? K: I'm great and you? O: Thanks to you, I am too. K: Way to go chief. And how's your health? O: It's fine thank God, it's fine. K: Are you working down there? O: Of course we are working?! A few have been caught by gunpoint or on mines. K: Good. Kill them all, God damn it. O: Everything, everything is going according to plan. K: Don't leave a single one alive. O: Everything is going according to plan. K: Way to go chief. The Turks are probably listening; Let them listen, the motherfuckers. O: Let them. They know what they can listen to. K: Right. Where is your boss? O: He went up towards you. K: When, this morning? O: Yes. K: OK. OK. Go on. We'll be in touch. O: Can I talk to Jevdjevic? K: Sure. O: Hello Jevdo? Which road should I use to send a truck in your direction to pick up some cattle? J: And where is that? O: Well, I don't know. My boss told me to ask you where most of them are. J: Well, the others have already grabbed everything and there's nothing left. O: The motherfuckers are worse than termites. J: Yes, now their code-names are Cowboy 1 and Cowboy 2. If your guys have caught some ... O: OK then, where are they? From Milici ... J: They're in the place where Legenda often carried out searches ... O: So, I should go to Milici ... J: ... Podravanje and up to Stublic. You'll find them there. You know the frequency and there are lots of soldiers and lots of sets, so you can call. O: Good. Bye. And that ends the reading of Prosecutor's Exhibit 787. Now, in this particular intercept, Witness Z, the parties identify themselves. One identifies himself as Krstic, and Obrenovic asks, "How are you, General, sir?" Before you intercepted this conversation, were you familiar with the voices of General Krstic and with Obrenovic's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you familiar with their voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Z [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we had been listening in to those frequencies for some time, and somehow the voice modulation enters your ear and one gets to be able to recognise them, because, after all, those people were important for us to listen in to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
